paras: The Cheneyville regulation of Black residents was a set of rules imposed on the Black population of Cheneyville, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, by a white mass meeting in August 1900 and enforced by a committee that ordered idle Black men to leave and closed their gathering places. The meeting followed the killing of a young white man, Bennie Wall, by a Black man, Joe Milton, whose lynching the parish sheriff prevented. Within days the committee had dive keepers ordered away and a young Black man publicly whipped, and the wire reported that "quite an emigration" had begun.

According to a New Orleans special to the New-York Tribune, Wall and a companion, Samuel Blum, met Milton and a young woman on a narrow plankwalk between Cheneyville and Theoda. The Tribune said Milton brushed heavily against Wall, Wall struck him, and the two then drew pistols and fired four shots each, killing Wall and breaking Milton's leg. A Cheneyville brief in the Age-Herald dated the shooting August 10, called the Black man "Joseph Hamilton," and said the cause was unknown.

A crowd of whites gathered, and armed squads from Bunkie, Alexandria, Lamourie and other places rode into Cheneyville offering their help, but the sheriff of Rapides Parish refused to allow a lynching. Milton was taken to jail at Alexandria, and the Tribune later reported that he had died after an operation on his leg.

The white residents then held a conference, with C. Cannon in the chair and R. H. Jackson as secretary, and a committee of five drafted resolutions. In the text printed by the Tribune and two Louisiana weeklies, the first resolution notified Black men with "no visible means of gaining a livelihood" to provide for themselves or be "compelled to leave"; the wire summary said simply that idle Black men were ordered out. Other articles pledged to break up gambling places, take pistols from Black men who fired them, end gatherings at the depot, and "severely" punish any "saucy and impudent" young Black man or woman who failed to yield the sidewalk to white women and children. A sixth resolution called nine-tenths of the ward's Black population law-abiding and promised them protection in return for their cooperation.

A committee of twenty-two was appointed to enforce the rules, and it closed a number of places where Black residents gathered and warned idle men to leave town. Several "dive" keepers were ordered away. On August 15, according to a New Orleans dispatch, the committee had a young Black man, Walter Brown, who had got in the way of white passengers on a train, marched to the business centre and given fifty lashes with a cowhide whip before a large crowd of white and Black onlookers.
The wire reported that an emigration of Black residents began at once, though no report gives how many left. No arrest or official action against the committee appears in the coverage.

The story reached northern and southern papers mainly through a New Orleans wire headed "TO REGULATE NEGROES' CONDUCT" in the New York Sun and "WHITES REGULATE BLACKS" in the Washington Times, reprinted in Alexandria, Virginia, and Raleigh. The wire called the armed visitors "regulators" and closed by noting Cheneyville's association with "Uncle Tom's Cabin." The New-York Tribune printed the resolutions under "TO RESTRAIN WORTHLESS NEGROES," and two days later an editorial paragraph set aside their "law, morals or propriety" to mock their grammar.

Louisiana weeklies approved. The Weekly Iberian headed its account "Another Bad Coon," linked the shooting to "the terrible fate of the negro Charles," and called the resolutions excellent, warning that idle men who did not reform "will be driven out." The Lafayette Gazette described them as written "in a conservative spirit" and suited to many Louisiana towns. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

Accounts of the shooting differ in detail, and all come from white papers: the Tribune said Milton brushed against Wall and Wall struck first, the Iberian that Wall knocked him down for "deliberately jostling him," and the Lafayette Gazette that Milton disputed Wall's right of way. The date of the shooting is given as August 10 by the Age-Herald and August 11 by the Tribune and the Iberian.

bases: A white mass meeting ordered idle Black men to find work or leave, closed their gathering places, and set a committee that warned idle men out of town and publicly whipped a Black man (A3, A5, A6).

The New Orleans wire (A3, A4), a separate Tribune report (A5), the Evening Times (A6) and two Louisiana weeklies printing the resolutions (A10, A11, A12) agree that the meeting adopted rules for Black residents and that a committee enforced them; the whipping rests on A6 alone.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: After Wall's killing, armed white squads offered to lynch Milton but the sheriff refused; a white conference then ordered idle Black men out of town, closed barrooms and gambling places, and named a committee of twenty-two, after which 'quite an emigration' began.

accounts.label: Tribune special and resolutions text
accounts.gist: Milton brushed against Wall on a narrow plankwalk, Wall struck him, and both drew pistols; the meeting's resolutions gave idle men the choice of finding sustenance or being compelled to leave.

accounts.label: Committee enforcement report
accounts.gist: The committee began work on August 14 and on August 15 had Walter Brown whipped fifty lashes before a crowd of white and Black onlookers.

accounts.label: Louisiana weeklies
accounts.gist: The Black man jostled Wall or disputed his right of way on the sidewalk and was knocked down; the papers printed the full resolutions and praised the town for not lynching.

framing.detail: The wire ran as 'TO REGULATE NEGROES' CONDUCT' and 'WHITES REGULATE BLACKS', calling the armed visitors 'regulators' and noting Cheneyville's tie to 'Uncle Tom's Cabin'.
The New-York Tribune headed the resolutions 'TO RESTRAIN WORTHLESS NEGROES' and two days later ridiculed their 'wonderfully and fearfully bad grammar' while declining to judge their law or morals.
The Evening Times reported the public whipping under 'A NEGRO DISCIPLINED.' without comment.

The Weekly Iberian headed its report 'Another Bad Coon.', called the resolutions 'excellent', and said idle Black men who did not reform would be 'driven out'; the Lafayette Gazette called them 'conservative' and fit for many Louisiana towns.

conflicts.note: A1 is a Cheneyville-datelined brief; A2 is a New Orleans special and A10 a Louisiana weekly. The Tribune of August 14 (A5) puts the killing 'three days ago'.
Only the first brief uses Hamilton; all later reports say Milton.

versions.value: Milton brushed against Wall on a narrow plankwalk; Wall struck him; Milton walked off, drew a revolver, and both fired
The white man knocked the Black man down for 'deliberately jostling him'
The Black man disputed Wall's right of way and they exchanged shots

conflicts.note: All versions come from white papers; none gives Milton's account. Each agrees Wall struck or knocked down Milton before the shooting, except A12, which does not say.

versions.value: Notified to provide means of sustenance or be compelled to leave

conflicts.note: The resolutions' text (A5, A10, A12) is conditional; the wire summary states an outright order, and says the committee then warned idle men to leave.

versions.value: As the result of an operation on his leg
From wounds received in the exchange of shots

conflicts.note: Compatible: the leg wound came from Wall's bullet (A1, A2).

record_check.dossier: Committee of twenty-two to enforce (and five to draft); no report gives twenty-five.
Walter Brown, a young Black man, was whipped fifty lashes by order of the committee; idle men and dive keepers were ordered out.
Add a public whipping and the closing of barrooms and gambling places; the order to leave was conditional in the resolutions' text.
A lynching of Joe Milton was threatened by a crowd and by armed squads from nearby towns and prevented by the sheriff.
1900-08-13 is the wire dateline; the shooting was August 10 or 11, the meeting by August 13 (possibly Saturday, August 11), and the whipping August 15.
A white citizens' conference chaired by C. Cannon (secretary R. H. Jackson) and its enforcement committee.
No one was killed by the committee; the triggering shooting killed Bennie Wall (white), and Joe Milton (Black) later died of his leg wound after an operation.

info: Shooting of Wall on August 10 (A1) or August 11 (A2, A10); mass meeting held by August 13, 'Saturday last' per a paper of August 18; committee began work August 14; whipping of Walter Brown August 15.
Cheneyville, Louisiana; the shooting on a plankwalk between Cheneyville and Theoda.

Idle or unemployed Black men of the Cheneyville community (ordered to find work or leave); keepers of 'dives' and gambling places (ordered away, places closed); Walter Brown, a young Black man (whipped).

The resolutions charged 'a certain set of negro men' with having no visible means of livelihood, gambling, carrying concealed weapons and firing pistols, crowding the depot, and failing to yield sidewalks to white women and children; Brown was accused of getting in the way of white passengers on a train.
A conference or mass meeting of white citizens of Cheneyville, chaired by C. Cannon with R. H. Jackson as secretary, and the enforcement committee it appointed.
Joe Milton, wounded in the leg by Wall in the exchange of shots, died in custody after an operation on the leg; not killed by the mob.
The committee closed a number of places where Black residents gathered and warned idle men to leave; 'Quite an emigration set in at once.'
